description: 4 Astro 1 Bio 1 Math is a team of high school students with a high enthusiasm for science, technology, and space exploration. By combining our interests across various disciplines— we collaborate to solve real-world challenges with creative perspectives. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are determined to hone our critical thinking skills, broaden our horizons, and gain valuable experience that will serve as a strong foundation for our academic journey and future in the world of science.
summary:
Our project, “The Quiet Water of Cabeus,” is a web-based interactive storytelling platform that brings to life the overlooked stories of human-made objects left behind on the Moon’s surface. In this story, we’ve chosen LCROSS (Lunar Crater Observation and Sensing Satellite) as the main character. Through engaging narratives, users can explore the mission, objectives, journey, and scientific contributions of LCROSS and eleven other objects related to lunar exploration.

Instead of presenting conventional historical descriptions, we transform scientific and historical information into immersive stories, allowing each object to tell its own story. This interactive website aims to make space exploration more accessible, engaging, and enjoyable, especially for young audiences.

By highlighting the equipment and objects left behind on the Moon, our project preserves their historical and scientific value while fostering curiosity about humanity’s journey to Earth’s largest natural satellite. After all, even the objects left behind have stories worth telling and remembering.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Our project presents stories and information about human-made objects that were sent to the Moon and eventually left on its surface. The website uses a first-person storytelling approach, in which each object tells its own story, describing its mission, purpose, journey, and contributions. Supported by an engaging and interactive user interface (UI), we aim to make the history of lunar exploration easier to understand while sparking readers' interest, particularly among younger generations, in science and space exploration.

What benefits does it have? 

Upon server initialization, the system launches a start-up user interface (UI) while concurrently executing a database program designed to record and log user activity throughout the web session. Following this, the application initiates an interactive visual novel, serving as the primary narrative framework for user engagement. The experience is further enhanced through integrated audio storytelling, which provides atmospheric context and reinforces the thematic setting of the narrative. Additionally, the system presents scientific data pertaining to space instruments and artifacts that have impacted and remain on the lunar surface. 

Our project provides value by expanding knowledge in an engaging and enjoyable manner, offering readers a compelling experience regarding the spacecraft and artifacts that have reached the lunar surface. In particular, it facilitates school-aged children in accessing information and developing a clearer understanding of the various spacecraft and man-made objects that have descended upon the Moon. 

What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact of the project is to inspire curiosity and deepen young readers' understanding of lunar exploration by making knowledge about the spacecraft and man-made objects on the Moon accessible, engaging, and memorable. Specifically, it aims to:

  1. Increase awareness among school-aged children of the various spacecraft and artifacts that have reached the lunar surface.
  2. Foster a clearer understanding of humanity's presence on the Moon — moving beyond vague awareness to concrete knowledge.
  3. Spark interest in space, science, and history by presenting information in an enjoyable, age-appropriate way.
  4. Build a foundation for future learning by giving children an early, positive encounter with space exploration topics.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Tools: Claude AI, Gemini AI, Kilo AI, Z AI, DeepL

Coding language: Phyton, CSS, Javascript, HTML

Hardware: Laptop, Handphone, Microphone, Headset
Software: 

  • Writer: Google docx
  • Back End: Visual Studio Code (VS Code), Git, GitHub
  • Front End: Figma, FL Studio, Visual Studio Code (VS Code), GitHub

How is your project creative?

Our project demonstrates creativity through the development of an accessible platform that transforms conventional storytelling into an immersive experience. The innovative narrative personifies a human-made satellite on the lunar surface as the primary storyteller, giving voice to an otherwise inanimate object. This creative approach enables the narrative to unfold from a distinctive perspective, fostering a deeper emotional connection with the audience. Additionally, the design was carefully crafted to deliver visually compelling elements that bring the written narrative to life, thereby enhancing reader engagement and emotional resonance. The combination of a unique storytelling perspective and a striking visual presentation serves to elevate the written content, making it more impactful and memorable for the reader.

What factors did your team consider?

  1. Scientific accuracy. We built the story around what the mission actually found: LCROSS’s Centaur stage and Shepherding Spacecraft struck Cabeus crater on 9 October 2009, about four minutes apart, and the plume held roughly 155 kg of water vapour and ice. Each spacecraft panel gives its mission, fate and legacy and links to sources such as NASA and NSSDCA. Where we simplified, we said so on screen: visuals are artistic, not to scale, and locations are approximate. We also noted that LCROSS never left the Earth–Moon neighbourhood.
  2. Emotional storytelling with visual style. Many people find space history dry, so we gave LCROSS a first-person voice and a clear arc: a question, a sacrifice, then finding other abandoned spacecraft. The theme, “Abandoned, but not forgotten,” shapes the ending. We labelled the narrated sections as a work of fiction so the story is never mistaken for fact. We chose a storybook look with a dark, calm palette to suit a quiet, reflective subject.
  3. Which spacecraft to include and how to frame their fates. We chose missions that cover different eras and different space programmes, from Luna 2 (1959) and Apollo 11 to Chandrayaan-3 (2023). We distinguished planned endings (deliberate impacts, planned abandonment) from accidents (Vikram, 2019), and described each by what it taught us.
  4. Interaction that supports learning. Players travel along a path from star to star, separate the Centaur themselves, and rotate and zoom a 3D Moon to explore markers. A journey map lets them jump to any stage. “More Information” sections keep the main text short while giving depth to those who want it.
  5. Credits and permissions. We credited image sources (NASA, ISRO, Wikimedia Commons) and the Creative Commons BY 3.0 music licence.
  6. Cross-device readiness. The project is a single HTML file that runs in any modern browser on phones, tablets and desktops with nothing to install. The scene scales to any screen, adapts to rotation, supports touch, mouse and keyboard, and switches to a lighter mode on mobile devices so it stays smooth.
